extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of constitutional law and political theory; policymakers and constitutional designers
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing what constitutional arrangements (simple democracy, mixed government, standing powers, elections, judicial appointment, etc.) produce liberty, stability, and justice. The page argues normative criteria for designing and judging constitutions for states of differing size, wealth, and commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed government (mixture of monarchic, aristocratic, democratic elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: The constitution should combine monarchical, aristocratical, and democratical powers (e.g., 'the mixture of monarchical power in the kings and consuls, and the mixture of democratical power in the tribunes and popular assemblies...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A near equality among these ingredients produced the periods of greatest liberty, virtue, glory, and prosperity (examples: Rome, Carthage, Sparta). Each example cited demonstrates that a triple combination is more favorable than a simple democracy; when the balance is weakened the state hastens to ruin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid simple (pure) democracy for large, populous states
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple or purely representative democracy is unsuitable for states where the people are numerous, rich, and commerce is extensive: local small cantons may appear democratic but are mixtures in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No historical precedents support simple democracy for large modern polities (England, American states); small, narrow cantons (e.g., some Swiss cantons) are not models for large nations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect minorities against majority rule (risk of majority tyranny)
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom and justice in a simple democracy exist for the majority only; the minority will be discouraged, brow‑beaten, insulted, and without redress except by civil war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the majority controls determinations, judges, and juries, the minority remains within the reach of arbitrary disposition of the majority; constitutions must guard minority rights against the passions and interests of majorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of powers / checks and balances
rubrics_metrics.description: The sovereign authority (legislative, executive, judicial) should not be safely lodged in one assembly; standing and separate powers are necessary to prevent oppression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The majority and their leaders (principes populi) will oppress the minority if all powers are united; a system of distinct branches and mutual checks is required to preserve liberty and security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial independence and appointment safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: If judges are appointed by the majority, they will generally be the leaders' friends or partisans and will make law speak in favour of those who appoint them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard against packing judges and juries; ensure mechanisms that prevent the creation of judges whose function is to expound law to favour the ruling party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unanimity as an impractical basis for government
rubrics_metrics.description: No good government was ever founded upon the principle of unanimity in every vote, resolve, or law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requiring unanimity on all decisions would prevent governance; practical governments rely on majority decisions but must temper majority power with other protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition/limit on ex post facto and retroactive legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: Unchecked passions and interests of the majority will frequently produce ex post facto laws to mortify the minority and support their adversaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutions should constrain retroactive legislation and other measures that a ruling majority might use to punish or dispossess minorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of a distinct, standing executive authority
rubrics_metrics.description: A standing/hereditary head (king) as commander in chief and general may create an influence bordering on royal supremacy but contributes to balance and authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An executive distinct from the legislature provides unity of command and a stabilizing influence; its role should be balanced by other institutions to avoid tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of a standing senate or second chamber
rubrics_metrics.description: A distinct senate should be guardians of property against levellers, repository of national tradition and customs, and controllers in turn of both kings and representatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A second chamber protects property, institutional memory, and acts as a check on both the executive and popular representatives; its presence helps prevent rapid or factional change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election frequency and risk of venality/faction
rubrics_metrics.description: Annual elections of high magistrates and senators may introduce venality and convulsions; if annual elections cannot be supported they may be counterproductive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance frequency of elections against the risk of corruption and instability—longer terms or some standing offices may better preserve dignity and avoid electoral venality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practicality of constitutional provisions (fit to social/economic conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutional provisions that worked historically (e.g., Lycurgus's prohibitions on travel, commerce, and money) are impractical for modern peoples who value commerce and communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutions must account for contemporary social/economic realities; transplanting archaic or extreme constraints will fail in modern societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular consent as the source of political legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The original and fountain of all just power and government is in the people; the people have the right to erect any form (monarchy, aristocracy, democracy, or mixtures) if they judge it best for liberty and prosperity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legitimacy rests on popular adoption and the people's continuing right to interpose and depose for misadministration; this also implies people may choose standing powers if they judge them necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale-appropriate representation (geographic and numerical fit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Local towns or counties (e.g., 'the town of Berwick upon Tweed') cannot reasonably 'carve, judge, choose, and determine' for an entire kingdom; representation must account for scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design representation mechanisms that reflect the polity's size and heterogeneity; avoid allowing small localities to dominate national decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing powers as devices to avoid electoral evils
rubrics_metrics.description: Standing powers (hereditary or permanent elements) have been instituted to avoid greater evils: corruption, sedition, war, and bloodshed in elections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justify standing institutions as harm-minimizing measures where frequent or poorly structured elections would produce worse outcomes; but balance them with accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional rituals and reciprocal oaths to bind checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanisms such as regular mutual oaths (e.g., monthly oaths by kings and Ephori) create an indissoluble bond uniting different orders against encroachment by another chamber.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural bonds (oaths, rituals, formal obligations) can be used to formalize mutual restraints and maintain balances between branches or estates.
